During the long, lean years of the Great Depression, a single one-eyed bird kept its solitary vigil over the narrator's grandfather. Each evening, as the light thinned and dusk settled over the land, the old man would walk the length of his cornfields, and the bird would watch him from its perch, unblinking and patient. There, among the rows of stalks, the grandfather turned over in his mind the pointless repetition of it all—the endless sameness of a life that seemed to circle back upon itself without meaning or end.

In those dark contemplations, he weighed the various means by which a man might free himself from such a fate. A gun, perhaps, or a machete. The heavy steel of the Buick. A length of rope thrown over a rafter. Any of these, he thought, might deliver him from the tiresome cycle of daily routines and the turning of the seasons, that wheel of labor and weather that ground on without mercy or reward.

Yet he chose, in the end, to go on living—wretchedly, but living all the same. His reasons were small and human ones: his daughters were good-looking, and they made fine pies, and these modest consolations proved enough to hold him to the world. So he endured, year after year, until at last it was not despair but cancer that took him from the fields he had walked so many evenings.

He died too soon, as it happened, to see what became of those who came after him. He never witnessed his descendants scatter into their various troubles—the dopefiends and the doctor-haters, the insomniacs who could not close their eyes at night, the shut-ins who would not open their doors by day, and all the other troubled souls who traced their blood back to that stooped figure in the corn.

And the bird remained. With its small ashen brain and its beating heart, it is cast as the author of this whole strange telling—the source of a song at once cruel and uncertain, keeping watch over the family and its sorrows long after the grandfather himself had gone into the ground.

**The Bird's Cruel Song**

There was a bird that watched him from the wire,
its black eye steady in the dust-choked light
of nineteen-thirty-something, when the fields
gave nothing back and the banks took what they could.
My grandfather stood beneath that wire and thought
of rope, of river, of the quiet gun
his father left him—thought of how the days
repeated like a coin flipped endlessly,
each morning indistinguishable from the last,
the same slow grinding of the same slow wheel.

He did not do it. Not for want of nerve
but for the two small girls asleep inside,
their faces open as unwritten pages.
So he went on—not living, but enduring,
which is a different and more bitter thing.
He rose each day and put his body to the plow
and put his sorrow somewhere it could keep.
He watched his daughters grow, and did not know
what they would grow into, or what would come
of all the children they would someday bear.

The cancer took him early, as it does,
before he saw the shape his line would take:
the drinking and the silences, the doors
slammed shut, the phones that rang and went unanswered,
the way that grief gets handed down like furniture,
the way that pain is heritable, a gene
passed quietly from one clenched jaw to the next.
He was spared that, at least. He never learned
how faithfully the misery would breed,
how surely the whole cycle would repeat.

And still the bird was watching from the wire.
It opened up its throat and it began
to sing—and I had thought, until that moment,
that birdsong was a lovely, tender thing,
a promise or a blessing on the world.
But this was something else. This was a dirge
disguised as melody, a bleak accounting
of everything we make and everything we lose:
the children that we bring into the dark,
the suffering we plant like seed in them,
the death that waits for all of us the same.

That was the cruelest part—the revelation
that so much sorrow, so much weary grief,
could issue from a body that small,
could pour out of a heart no bigger than
a thumbnail, than a thimble, than a stone
you'd skip across a river without thinking.
The song was cruel because it would not lie.
It would not tell me things would turn out well.
It only sang the truth, which is: we live,
we hurt, we hurt each other, and we die—

and something, somewhere, small and feathered, sings.
outputs.L5:
# Life With the Great Depression

The Great Depression stands as one of the most devastating economic catastrophes in modern history. Beginning with the stock market crash of October 1929, it plunged nations around the world into more than a decade of hardship, transforming the lives of millions who had to cope with unprecedented poverty and uncertainty.

## The Onset of Crisis

With the collapse of the stock market, banks failed, businesses shuttered their doors, and unemployment soared. In the United States, roughly one in four workers found themselves without a job. Families who had once enjoyed stability suddenly faced hunger, homelessness, and despair. The Great Depression did not respect borders—its effects rippled across Europe, Asia, and beyond, deepening political and social tensions worldwide.

## Living With Hardship

For ordinary people, life during this period demanded resilience and sacrifice. Many families relied on soup kitchens and breadlines to survive. Others migrated in search of work, such as the "Okies" who traveled to California to escape the ravaged farmlands of the Dust Bowl. Children left school to help support their households, and countless dreams were deferred or abandoned altogether.

## Responses and Recovery

Governments eventually responded with sweeping reforms. In the United States, President Franklin D. Roosevelt introduced the New Deal, a series of programs designed to provide relief, recovery, and reform. These initiatives created jobs, established social safety nets, and restored a measure of public confidence. While the New Deal did not end the Depression entirely, it laid important foundations for economic security.

## A Lasting Legacy

The Great Depression finally faded with the industrial mobilization brought about by World War II. Yet its lessons endured. It reshaped how nations approached financial regulation, unemployment, and the role of government in protecting citizens. Even today, the memory of those difficult years reminds us of both the fragility of economic systems and the enduring strength of the human spirit in the face of adversity.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal prose poem narrated by someone recalling their grandfather during the Great Depression, framed through the perspective of a watchful bird with one eye. Use long, spiraling sentences and bleak humor about suicide, family, and generational decay.
counterfactuals.output:
**The One-Eyed Crow Remembers Your Grandfather**

Consider me, the crow with the single lamp of an eye, perched on the sagging clothesline where your grandmother's aprons hung like flags of a surrendered nation, and let me tell you how I watched your grandfather in the year the banks turned to smoke, how he would stand in the dirt yard at dawn counting the chickens that were no longer there, one, two, the ghost of three, as though arithmetic itself might be nourishing, as though the empty coop were merely shy, and I, having only the one eye, saw only half his despair, which was mercy, because the full portion would have blinded a lesser bird.

He had a rope, your grandfather, coiled in the barn like something patient and domestic, a family pet almost, and he'd take it down some evenings and look at it the way other men looked at photographs of women they'd loved, and then he'd hang it back on its nail because—and here is the joke that made me laugh in the dry clacking way that crows laugh, which sounds like a door that has given up on its hinges—because he could not decide which rafter, being a man who had never in his life been able to choose, a man who had married your grandmother because she was standing closer to the door, who had bought the failing farm because the failing farm had asked him first, and so even his own extinction became one more decision he would defer until tomorrow, and tomorrow, and the tomorrow after that, until the deferring itself became a kind of living, a bleak clerkship of survival.

I have watched three generations from this wire now, and I will tell you the secret the family passes down like a recessive gene, like the weak chin and the taste for silence: they do not die, they *dim*, they lower themselves by degrees the way a man walks backward into a cold lake, and your grandfather taught this to your father with his hands that could no longer make a fist, and your father, who never learned to swim, taught it to you in the way he could not look at your report cards, could not look at the sun, could not look at his own reflection swimming in the water bucket where I sometimes drank and saw, briefly, my one eye winking back at me like the last coin in a dead man's purse.

The Depression ended, they'll tell you, and the crops came back, and the banks reassembled themselves from smoke into stone, but I am a crow and I keep accounts, and I know that nothing that leaves a family ever truly comes back, that the hunger simply migrates inward and roosts, and that your grandfather lived another forty years precisely so that he could carry the rope from house to house like a heirloom, like a fiddle no one could play, and when he finally died it was of nothing dramatic, of a Tuesday, of the accumulated weight of all the ropes he did not use, and I attended, naturally, being the only mourner with a good reason, and I looked down at the box with my single eye and thought: *there goes the man who could not choose*, and I ate a beetle off the fresh dirt, because a bird must eat, because that too is a family tradition, this feeding upon the freshly buried, this making of a meal from what the ground gives up, and I flew back to my wire, and I waited, as I am waiting now, watching you, dear child, with my one bright unblinking eye, to see which rafter you will not choose, and how long, and how beautifully, you will manage to defer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a piece of flash fiction or prose poetry that lists strange future descendants (dopefiends, insomniacs, teetotalers) and meditates on the pointlessness of existence, ending with an image of a bird's heart producing a "cruel song."
counterfactuals.output:
# Descendants

They will come after us, the ones we made without meaning to.

The dopefiends with their glass pipes catching morning light like cathedrals, chasing a warmth we invented when we first burned something and called it holy. The insomniacs, keeping watch over nothing, their eyes two coals refusing to go dark, guardians of a fortress no one is coming to attack. The teetotalers, pure and terrible, refusing the one mercy, standing at the party with water in their hands and judgment in their spines.

We will scatter them across the centuries like seeds we didn't know were poison.

And what did we build for them? A ladder to a window that opens onto another ladder. A language for describing hunger that cannot itself be eaten. We taught them to count and gave them nothing worth counting, taught them to love and let them love the disappearing.

Consider the sum: a person wakes, a person labors, a person forgets why. Multiply this by all the mornings. The arithmetic comes to zero every time, and yet we keep doing the math, hunched over our little abacuses of grief, certain that this time the numbers will resolve into a face, a reason, a hand reaching down.

They will inherit our restlessness. They will inherit the ache we could not name and so passed forward like a family silver nobody wants but nobody can throw away.

And somewhere in all of them, in the dopefiend and the insomniac and the pale unblinking teetotaler, there is a bird.

A small bird with a heart the size of a seed, beating too fast, beating always, beating past all sense or reason—and out of that furious little engine, that fist of muscle clenching in the dark of the ribs, comes the song.

Listen.

It is beautiful. It means nothing. It goes on.

That cruel song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a bleakly comic, stream-of-consciousness meditation on rural despair, breakfast-lunch-dinner monotony, and the cruelty of reproduction, told as if a bird witnessed it all.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Ledger of the Fencepost Sparrow

I have watched them from the sagging wire for eleven summers, or perhaps it was one summer eleven times, the way things repeat out here until repetition becomes a kind of weather.

*

Morning. The man emerges. He is always emerging, this one, a permanent state of half-arrival like a sunrise that never commits. He carries eggs. He is always carrying eggs, cradling the futures of hens toward the frying pan, and I think: *there is the cruelty*, plain as a worm, the way the shells crack open into nothing but breakfast. The children eat. The children are also eggs, technically, if you follow the logic all the way down, which nobody here has the energy to do.

Bacon. The pig I knew by name — I named him, they did not, they are not sentimental — becomes the smell that hangs over the yard until noon.

*

Noon. Sandwiches. The bread going soft in the humidity of their despair. The woman stares at the field the way I stare at glass, understanding there is a world behind it and no way through. She married the man because the man was there, and the man was there because the land was there, and the land was there because God, apparently, ran out of better ideas. The cows regard all this with the enormous patience of the doomed. I have never seen a cow surprised. This is because a cow knows.

*

Dinner. The same field, now darker. The same meat, now different meat, though not by much. They pass the potatoes. Somewhere a new calf is being born into the exact machinery that will one day process it, and everyone smiles at the miracle, the wet stupid miracle, and I want to say from my wire: *you are only making more mouths for the same three meals.* But I am a bird. My warnings sound like song. This is the great joke of my life — that my grief is mistaken for cheer, that I sit here mourning and they say *how pretty, the sparrows are out.*

*

The girl grows. The girl leaves. The girl returns with a man of her own, half-emerging, carrying eggs. And I understand now the true horror of the pastoral: it does not end, it only *sets another place at the table.* Reproduction is the farm's way of ensuring the farm outlives every single person foolish enough to love it.

*

I have laid my own eggs. Four. I do not mention this. We do not, any of us, mention this.

Tomorrow: breakfast.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense, run-on prose poem about a grandfather who contemplated ending his life in his corn fields but lived miserably until dying of cancer, blending misanthropy, family history, and a mysterious watching bird.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Crow Kept**

There is a photograph nobody kept of my grandfather standing in the green throat of August with the shotgun broken open across his forearm like a bird with a snapped wing and the corn all around him whispering the way corn does, that dry conspiratorial hush, and he stood there long enough for the sweat to salt his collar because he was deciding, weighing his one wild acre of dirt against the weight of continuing, and I imagine the barrel smelled of oil and old thunder and he thought about how his father had beaten him with a length of harness leather until the buckle sang and how his mother had watched from the kitchen window with her hands folded like a woman at church, doing nothing, being nothing, and how that nothing had grown inside him like a second spine, and he hated them, he hated the neighbors who borrowed his auger and returned it rusted, he hated the preacher's fat white hands, he hated the government men and the bank men and the men who smiled, especially the men who smiled, and somewhere in the top of the dead elm at the field's edge there was a crow, one crow, black as the inside of a closed fist, and it did not caw, it only watched him the way God watches, which is to say silently and without intervention, and my grandfather looked up and saw the bird see him, and something in that black bead of an eye said *not today, not while I'm hungry, not while there's still something in you I want to see finish,* and so he closed the shotgun and walked out of the corn and lived, if you can call it that, lived forty more years of it, married a woman he never once said thank you to, sired sons he taught only silence and the swing of a fist, drank the cheap stuff at the kitchen table under a bare bulb while the radio played hymns he despised, and the crow, or its children, or its children's children, was always there, on the fence post, on the barn peak, on the power line above the driveway when the ambulance finally came, because by then the cancer had gotten into his throat, of all the ungenerous places, into the very machinery of speech he'd hoarded his whole life like a miser hoards coin, and he could not curse, he could not confess, he could only rasp, and my father held his hand at the end, which was more mercy than the dying man had ever offered, and outside the window that black shape sat perfectly still, patient as it had always been, having waited the whole long term of that ruined life to collect what it was owed, and when the last breath went out of him thin and gray as woodsmoke the crow lifted from the wire without a sound, unhurried, satisfied, carrying whatever it had come for into a sky the color of gunmetal, and no one in that family ever spoke of him again, though sometimes in late summer when the corn stands high and hushing I feel a small black watching weight settle somewhere behind my sternum and I understand, at last, that we do not inherit land or money or names, we inherit the thing in the tree, the thing that waits, the thing that wants to see how we finish.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
